screens.title: Advanced Aggregation Techniques
screens.subtitle: Persisting results with $out, merging with $merge, and multi-view analysis with $facet

narration.text: In this lesson we'll explore three advanced aggregation stages that extend MongoDB's Aggregation Framework beyond read-only analysis. First, $out writes an entire pipeline result to a collection, creating or replacing that collection; it's useful for materialized views and full-report regeneration. Second, $merge lets you atomically insert, update, or replace documents in an existing collection with several merge strategies, making it the right choice for incremental updates and safe upserts. Third, $facet runs multiple independent sub-pipelines over the same input and returns a single document containing each sub-result, which is ideal for dashboards and multi-perspective queries. You will see concrete examples: creating a monthly sales summary with $out, updating a dailySales collection with $merge, and producing category summaries and top products with $facet. I'll also highlight safety concerns: $out overwrites data and must be the last stage, $merge requires careful choice of on/whenMatched/whenNotMatched behaviors, and $facet can consume memory when sub-pipelines are heavy. By the end, you will know which stage to pick for reporting, upserts, or multi-analysis and how to avoid common mistakes. Consider how persistent outputs change operational workflows and testing practices when you design pipelines.

keyIdea.title: What you'll learn
keyIdea.text: $out creates or replaces a collection; $merge atomically updates/inserts with merge strategies; $facet runs multiple sub-pipelines and returns a single document of arrays.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.6 › Advanced Aggregation Techniques
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

Advanced Aggregation Techniques

Learn how to persist aggregation output, perform atomic merges, and run parallel analyses in a single pipeline.

In this lesson
$out, $merge, $facet basics and examples
Coming up
Safety notes, merge strategies, and multi-faceted analytics
Hands-on
A $facet exercise with customerReviews
Why this matters

Persisting aggregation results and merging them safely is essential when analytics need to be consumed by other systems, or when results must be re-used without recomputing. Multi-faceted aggregation saves round trips for dashboards and ensures consistency between related views.

Tip: think carefully about how data replacement or merges affect downstream consumers and backups.
Visual summary
$out
Write pipeline output and replace target collection
$merge
Controlled inserts/updates into existing collection
$facet
Parallel sub-pipelines, single combined output
Explore Key Topics
Materialized views: recreate with $out when full overwrite is acceptable.
Incremental updates: prefer $merge to change or augment documents atomically.
Multi-faceted analytics: use $facet to run several analyses in one query and return a single document.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: What you'll be able to do after this chapter

narration.text: By the end of this chapter you will be able to choose the correct aggregation stage for persisting or updating results, design sub-pipelines for multi-faceted analysis, and avoid common pitfalls. Objective one is to utilize the $out stage to write pipeline results to a new collection: you will learn when overwriting an entire collection is appropriate and how $out must be the final stage. Objective two is to employ $merge for atomic writes to an existing collection; you'll understand parameters such as into, on, whenMatched, and whenNotMatched and how they enable safe upserts and replacements. Objective three is to understand the purpose and structure of $facet: you'll see how multiple independent sub-pipelines produce arrays inside a single document and why that’s useful for dashboards. Objective four is to design pipelines combining $facet with other stages to produce multiple analytics from the same input, and to recognize memory and structure considerations. Each objective includes a practical competency milestone so you can verify readiness: recreating a materialized view, safely updating a daily collection with $merge, composing a three-branch $facet, and comparing $out versus $merge trade-offs in a real scenario. These skills change how you design reporting and operational analytics in MongoDB.

screens.title: $out stage: definition and primary behavior
screens.subtitle: $out writes pipeline results and replaces the target collection

narration.text: The $out stage is a straightforward way to persist the result of an aggregation into a collection. Conceptually it takes the documents produced by the pipeline and writes them to a specified collection: if that collection does not exist, $out creates it; if it does exist, $out replaces its entire contents. That replacement behavior makes $out suitable for materialized views, nightly reports, or full-refresh workflows that do not require merging with previous state. Remember: $out must be the final stage in the pipeline—any stage after $out is invalid. A concrete example from our chapter stores daily grouped sales into a monthlySalesSummary collection. Run carefully: if monthlySalesSummary already exists, $out deletes whatever was in there and writes the new results, which can be destructive if you expected incremental behavior. A common misconception is to treat $out like a safe upsert; it is not. If you need to preserve, merge, or partially update existing documents, choose $merge instead. Key takeaway: use $out when you intend a deterministic, complete replacement of the target collection, and always confirm your backup and timing policies before running it in production.

keyIdea.title: $out summary
keyIdea.text: $out creates or replaces the target collection and must be the last pipeline stage. Use for full-refresh materialized outputs.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.6 › $out: Definition
Definition

What $out does

It writes the aggregation result into the named collection and replaces its contents if the collection already exists. Use it for complete refreshes and materialized views.

Must be the last stage; creates collection if missing.
Danger: existing collection data is overwritten.
Good for scheduled reports and archive transformations.
Example
db.sales.aggregate([
  { $match: { date: { $gte: ISODate("2023-11-01T00:00:00Z"), $lt: ISODate("2023-12-01T00:00:00Z") } } },
  { $group: {
      _id: { $dateToString: { format: "%Y-%m-%d", date: "$date" } },
      totalRevenue: { $sum: { $multiply: ["$price", "$quantity"] } },
      totalItems: { $sum: "$quantity" }
    }
  },
  { $sort: { _id: 1 } },
  { $out: "monthlySalesSummary" }
])
Key Takeaway

$out is simple but destructive: use it when you want a deterministic full rewrite of the target collection.

screens.title: Safe usage patterns and common mistakes with $out
screens.subtitle: Avoid accidental data loss when using $out

narration.text: Using $out without careful operational controls is one of the most common sources of unexpected data loss in aggregation workflows. The $out stage replaces the entire target collection when it runs, so the first safety rule is to never run $out against a production collection unless you intentionally want full replacement. A second rule is to maintain backups or use versioned collection names (for example, monthlySalesSummary_2023_11) so the previous snapshot remains available. Third, do your testing on a staging namespace and confirm that your pipeline result shape matches the target schema and indexes you expect. A common mistake is treating $out like an incremental write: engineers sometimes forget that it does not merge, upsert, or preserve existing metadata. If you require incremental changes or merges, use $merge with appropriate on and whenMatched options. Also consider access control and the timing of scheduled jobs: a nightly $out run should occur when downstream consumers will tolerate a brief period of replacement. In short, plan, backup, and prefer non-destructive workflows unless a full refresh is the explicit goal. When in doubt, prototype your $out pipeline into a temporary collection first.

keyIdea.title: Safety checklist
keyIdea.text: Back up before $out, use versioned target names for snapshots, test in staging, and prefer $merge for incremental updates.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.6 › $out Safety
Common Mistakes
  • Running $out on a production collection without backups.
  • Expecting $out to merge or upsert existing documents.
  • Scheduling $out at times when consumers expect uninterrupted availability.
Practical mitigations include creating timestamped collection names, running the pipeline in staging first, and validating document shapes before overwriting.
Checklist before running $out
Confirm backup or snapshot exists
Test pipeline output schema and indexes
Use versioned target names if you need history
Run in staging or to a temp collection first
Common Mistake

Treating $out as an upsert stage. It replaces the entire target collection; switch to $merge for atomic merges and upserts.

screens.title: $merge stage: purpose and parameters
screens.subtitle: Atomically write results into an existing collection with flexible strategies

narration.text: The $merge stage was introduced to address scenarios where you need atomic, controlled writes back into an existing collection. Unlike $out, $merge does not indiscriminately replace the target collection. Instead it supports a set of parameters that govern how each aggregation result document interacts with the target collection. The core options are into, on, whenMatched, and whenNotMatched. Into can be a string or an object specifying a database and collection. On is the field or fields used to match existing documents; if omitted, _id is used. whenMatched determines what happens when a match is found: replace, keepExisting, merge, fail, or pipeline. Merge is the default and will combine fields from the aggregation output into the existing document, overwriting colliding fields. WhenNotMatched controls what happens when no match exists: insert, discard, or fail, with insert as the default. $merge supports writing to sharded collections, and because it operates document-by-document, it is far safer than $out for incremental workflows. A typical use case is updating a dailySales collection with new daily totals: match on the computed _id, merge if present, insert if missing. Choosing the right whenMatched strategy matters: replace discards previous fields; merge preserves non-conflicting fields; pipeline gives full control via a small update pipeline.

keyIdea.title: $merge parameters
keyIdea.text: into, on, whenMatched, whenNotMatched control matching and write behavior; choose them deliberately for safe, atomic updates.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.6 › $merge: Parameters
Parameter reference
  • into: target collection or { db, coll }.
  • on: the join key(s) used to match docs; defaults to _id.
  • whenMatched: replace, keepExisting, merge, fail, pipeline.
  • whenNotMatched: insert, discard, fail.
Choosing whenMatched matters. merge preserves other fields and only overwrites collisions; replace discards the previous document entirely. pipeline gives fine-grained control via an update pipeline when needed.
Example pattern
db.sales.aggregate([
  { $match: { date: { $gte: ISODate("2023-11-20T00:00:00Z") } } },
  { $group: {
      _id: { $dateToString: { format: "%Y-%m-%d", date: "$date" } },
      dailyRevenue: { $sum: { $multiply: ["$price", "$quantity"] } },
      dailyItems: { $sum: "$quantity" }
    }
  },
  { $merge: {
      into: "dailySales",
      on: "_id",
      whenMatched: "merge",
      whenNotMatched: "insert"
    }
  }
])
Key Takeaway

$merge gives controlled, atomic writes and is the safer choice for incremental updates compared with $out.

screens.title: $out vs $merge
screens.subtitle: When to overwrite and when to merge

narration.text: Comparing $out and $merge helps you choose the correct persistence strategy. $out overwrites the target collection. Use it when you want a deterministic snapshot and do not need prior state. It is simple and often faster for full-refresh jobs, but destructive. $merge, by contrast, performs document-level operations controlled by into, on, whenMatched, and whenNotMatched. It is ideal for incremental updates where you want to update existing documents, preserve unrelated fields, or insert new documents. A concrete scenario clarifies the choice: if you are producing an 'All-Time Top 100 Products' report that reorders and changes entries daily and you do not need previous entries preserved, $out is an appropriate choice because rewriting the collection is simpler. But if you maintain a dailySensorData collection where each day’s document stores multiple computed fields and you only want to add new computed fields while preserving others, $merge with whenMatched: merge and whenNotMatched: insert is the correct tool. A common misconception is to assume $out is always faster—performance depends on data size, indexing, and whether you need incremental behavior. Always match the persistence model to operational requirements and data retention policies.

keyIdea.title: Choose by intent
keyIdea.text: $out for full-rewrite snapshots; $merge for controlled, incremental updates and atomic upserts.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.6 › $out vs $merge
$out

Full replacement

  • Creates or replaces the target collection.
  • Must be the last pipeline stage.
  • Good for materialized views or full reports.
Misconception: $out is not an upsert. It destroys previous data in the target collection.
$merge

Controlled merges

  • Atomically insert or update by match key.
  • Supports merge strategies and pipelines.
  • Better for incremental and upsert scenarios.
Misconception: $merge always preserves everything. Behavior depends on whenMatched strategy.
Decision rule

If you need a deterministic snapshot and do not need prior document state, use $out. If you need atomic, document-level updates or upserts, use $merge with explicit match and strategy.

screens.title: $facet stage: purpose and output structure
screens.subtitle: Run multiple independent sub-pipelines and return a single combined document

narration.text: The $facet stage allows you to run several independent aggregation pipelines on the same input simultaneously and gather their results into a single document. Each sub-pipeline in a $facet block processes the entire input set and produces an array. The overall output is a single document whose fields map to the names of the sub-pipelines, each containing an array of results. This structure is ideal for dashboards where you want different views—like totals, top items, and averages—derived from the same dataset without issuing multiple separate queries. A concrete example computes salesByCategory, top5Products, and avgPricePerCategory in one query. Be mindful that each facet sub-pipeline processes the whole input; for large datasets or heavy sub-pipelines this can lead to high memory usage. A common mistake is to expect $facet to stream or to filter early in each branch; instead, consider pushing restrictive stages like $match to the top of the shared pipeline so every facet receives a smaller input. Also remember subsequent stages see the single document shape returned by $facet; you may need to $unwind or $project fields accordingly. Key takeaway: $facet consolidates multiple analyses into one execution, improving consistency and reducing round trips when used carefully.

keyIdea.title: $facet summary
keyIdea.text: $facet runs multiple sub-pipelines over the same input and returns one document with arrays for each sub-result; plan for memory and output shape.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.6 › $facet: Purpose
Behavior

Each named sub-pipeline processes the same input set and produces an array. The $facet output is one document with fields matching sub-pipeline names.

Good for dashboards that need multiple related metrics at once.
Remember to reduce input with top-level $match where possible.
Be aware of memory usage for large inputs.
Example
db.products.aggregate([
  { $facet: {
      "salesByCategory": [
        { $group: { _id: "$category", totalQuantity: { $sum: "$quantity" } } },
        { $sort: { totalQuantity: -1 } }
      ],
      "top5Products": [
        { $sort: { quantity: -1 } },
        { $limit: 5 },
        { $project: { _id: 0, name: 1, quantity: 1 } }
      ],
      "avgPricePerCategory": [
        { $group: { _id: "$category", averagePrice: { $avg: "$price" } } }
      ]
    }
  }
])
Key Takeaway

$facet returns a single document of arrays. Use it to produce multiple consistent views in one query, but watch input size and memory.

screens.title: Practical $merge example: updating dailySales
screens.subtitle: Walk through a pipeline that merges daily totals into an existing collection

narration.text: Let's walk through a practical $merge pipeline that computes daily totals and updates a dailySales collection. First, the pipeline filters recent sales with $match to reduce the input and improve performance. Next, $group computes the daily totals, assembling a document whose _id is the date string and with fields dailyRevenue and dailyItems. After sorting if desired, the $merge stage writes results into dailySales using into: dailySales and on: _id. WhenMatched set to merge ensures new fields are combined into the existing document rather than replacing it entirely. WhenNotMatched set to insert creates a new document if no match exists. This pattern is safe for incremental workflows: existing documents gain new fields or updated values while unrelated fields remain. A common misconception is to assume merge will always preserve nested fields intelligently; in reality, field-level collisions overwrite simple field values, so plan field names carefully. Also consider index requirements: matching on _id is efficient, but if you choose other keys, ensure the target collection has appropriate indexes to avoid performance pitfalls. Finally, test your pipeline on a copy or in staging to validate merge semantics before running in production.

keyIdea.title: Merge pattern
keyIdea.text: Compute keys and aggregate fields, then $merge into the target collection with explicit on and whenMatched/whenNotMatched choices.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.6 › $merge Walkthrough
Pipeline excerpt
db.sales.aggregate([
  { $match: { date: { $gte: ISODate("2023-11-20T00:00:00Z") } } },
  { $group: {
      _id: { $dateToString: { format: "%Y-%m-%d", date: "$date" } },
      dailyRevenue: { $sum: { $multiply: ["$price", "$quantity"] } },
      dailyItems: { $sum: "$quantity" }
    }
  },
  { $merge: {
      into: "dailySales",
      on: "_id",
      whenMatched: "merge",
      whenNotMatched: "insert"
    }
  }
])
Notes & pitfalls
  • WhenMatched: merge overwrites colliding fields but preserves others.
  • If you need to replace entire documents, use replace as whenMatched.
  • Ensure match keys are indexed for performance.
Key Takeaway

$merge supports safe, atomic incremental updates. Validate semantics on a staging collection before production runs.

screens.title: $facet in practice: designing multi-faceted pipelines
screens.subtitle: How to compose branches and manage input size and output shape

narration.text: When designing a $facet pipeline, think in three parts: reduce input, design each facet branch, and shape the combined output. First, place restrictive stages such as $match or selective $project at the top of the shared pipeline to limit the documents each sub-pipeline receives. This reduces memory and work for every facet. Second, design each branch to be independent and return the array structure you need—one branch may group and sort, another may project top-N items, and a third may compute averages. Third, consider how you will consume the single-document output. You might leave it as a consolidated document for a dashboard consumer, or you may $unwind a specific array for further processing. A concrete pattern: for the customerReviews scenario, push an early $match if you only need recent reviews, then in $facet create avgRatings, totalReviews, and poorReviewProducts. Remember that because each branch sees the same input, duplicative heavy operations across branches can be costly; sometimes it's better to compute an intermediate reduced set into a temporary collection when branches diverge widely. Also verify the structure of arrays in the $facet output: subsequent stages must reference fields like results. avgRatings or directly the facet field names depending on your pipeline. Always test with representative data to estimate memory impact and response shape.

keyIdea.title: Design rule
keyIdea.text: Reduce the shared input early, keep branches focused and independent, and plan how you will consume the single document of arrays returned by $facet.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.6 › Designing $facet
Three-step process
  1. Reduce input: top-level $match or $project to shrink the dataset before branching.
  2. Design branches: each sub-pipeline should produce the array shape you need, like top-N or grouped summaries.
  3. Consume output: plan to use the single document of arrays directly or to $unwind specific arrays for further pipeline stages.
If branches share expensive computations, consider pre-aggregating into a temporary collection to avoid repeated work across facets.
Example branches
avgRatings: group by productId and compute average.
totalReviews: group by productId and count reviews.
poorReviewProducts: match rating 1 then group to distinct productIds.
Key Takeaway

Design $facet branches to avoid duplicated heavy work and always limit the shared input as early as possible.

screens.title: CustomerReviews $facet exercise
screens.subtitle: Complete the starter pipelines for avgRatings, totalReviews, and poorReviewProducts

narration.text: This hands-on example uses the customerReviews collection to show how $facet combines three analyses into one output. The starter dataset includes productId and rating values. Your task is to create three sub-pipelines inside $facet: avgRatings should group by productId and compute the average of rating; totalReviews should group by productId and compute a sum of one for the count; poorReviewProducts should match rating equal to 1, group by productId to collect distinct product IDs, and project only the productId. When the pipeline runs, $facet returns a single document with fields avgRatings, totalReviews, and poorReviewProducts, each an array. Inspect the arrays: avgRatings contains documents with _id equal to productId and an average field; totalReviews contains documents with reviewCount; poorReviewProducts contains at least the productIds that had poor ratings. A common oversight is forgetting to name the facet pipelines or to push an early $match to reduce input; both reduce memory and clarify the output shape. After you run this pipeline, consider how you might persist the results—use $out if you want a full snapshot, or use $merge to incrementally update a materialized analytics collection depending on operational needs. This exercise reinforces $facet structure and its practical consumption.

keyIdea.title: Exercise outcome
keyIdea.text: A single document containing avgRatings, totalReviews, and poorReviewProducts arrays that can be inspected or persisted as needed.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.6 › CustomerReviews $facet
Starter Data
db.customerReviews.insertMany([
  { "_id": 1, "productId": "PROD001", "rating": 5, "comment": "Excellent!" },
  { "_id": 2, "productId": "PROD002", "rating": 3, "comment": "Decent." },
  { "_id": 3, "productId": "PROD001", "rating": 4, "comment": "Very good." },
  { "_id": 4, "productId": "PROD003", "rating": 1, "comment": "Terrible." }
]);
Starter $facet
db.customerReviews.aggregate([
  { $facet: {
      "avgRatings": [ /* group by productId and compute $avg here */ ],
      "totalReviews": [ /* group by productId and $sum: 1 here */ ],
      "poorReviewProducts": [ /* match rating:1 then group and project productId */ ]
    }
  }
]);
After filling each sub-pipeline, run the aggregation and inspect the single-document result. Decide whether to persist with $out or $merge based on whether you need a full rewrite or incremental updates.
Instructor Hint

Name each facet clearly and validate array shapes. If the input is large, add a top-level $match to limit documents processed by each branch.

screens.title: Operational considerations: indexing, sharding, and performance
screens.subtitle: How $out, $merge, and $facet interact with operational constraints

narration.text: When you persist or merge aggregation results, consider how indexing, sharding, and pipeline design affect performance and correctness. For $merge, the match key you choose—often _id—should be indexed in the target collection to avoid full-collection scans on write. $merge supports writing to sharded collections, but you should ensure that the chosen shard key and into configuration match your cluster topology. For $out, remember that replacing a collection may drop indexes and require re-creating them if your workflow depends on specific indexes; also consider permissions: $out can create collections which requires suitable privileges. With $facet, performance concerns focus on memory and duplicate work: each branch processes the same input, so pushing a $match early is critical. If branches are extremely different or expensive, consider precomputing a reduced dataset. Also think about transactional semantics and atomicity: $merge provides atomic, document-level semantics for individual writes, while $out is a single operation that replaces the collection atomically from the user's perspective but will not merge. Finally, monitor jobs for memory usage when using $facet and schedule heavier refresh operations at off-peak times to reduce impact on the cluster. These operational choices determine reliability and performance in production systems.

keyIdea.title: Operational rule
keyIdea.text: Index match keys, understand sharding implications, and watch memory for $facet; recreate indexes after $out when necessary.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.6 › Operational Considerations
Checklist
  • Index the match key used by $merge to avoid costly lookups.
  • Confirm into and shard configurations when writing to sharded targets.
  • Recreate indexes if they are dropped or lost after $out operations.
  • Push restrictive filters before $facet to limit memory usage.
  • Schedule heavy refreshes during low-traffic windows and monitor memory.
Quick tips
Test merge semantics in staging to verify field-level overwrites.
Use timestamped collections for $out to keep historical snapshots if needed.
If facets are heavy, compute an intermediate reduced collection first.
Key Takeaway

Operational choices—indexes, sharding, scheduling, and testing—determine whether $out, $merge, or $facet behave safely and performantly in production.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.subtitle: What to remember from this chapter

narration.text: Let's summarize the core ideas to remember. First, $out writes pipeline results to a collection and replaces that collection if it exists; it's best for deterministic full-refresh snapshots and must be the last stage. Second, $merge provides atomic, document-level control for writing into an existing collection; configure into, on, whenMatched, and whenNotMatched to achieve the desired upsert or replace behavior. Third, $facet runs multiple independent sub-pipelines on the same input and returns a single document with arrays for each sub-result; use it for dashboards and multi-perspective analytics but be cautious about memory usage. Additional concepts include materialized views, which are pre-computed collections built via $out or maintained with $merge, and merge strategy choices that determine whether fields are merged, replaced, or cause a failure. Finally, always plan backups, index match keys, reduce input before facets, and test in staging. These practices help you design pipelines that are both powerful and safe in production environments.

keyIdea.title: Three core takeaways
keyIdea.text: $out replaces collections, $merge atomically updates/inserts, $facet produces multiple results in one document — choose based on intent and safety.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.6 › Key Concepts
$out Stage
Writes results and replaces target collection; final stage only.
$merge Stage
Atomic inserts/updates with into, on, whenMatched, and whenNotMatched options.
$facet Stage
Runs parallel sub-pipelines on the same input and returns a single document with arrays.
Summary Takeaway

Pick $out for deterministic full refreshes, $merge for incremental, atomic updates, and $facet to produce multiple analytics in a single query while minding memory.

screens.title: Key Concepts — Quick Reference
screens.subtitle: Three compact reminders and a closing thought

narration.text: Keep these three concise reminders in mind as you apply these stages. First, $out replaces the target collection and is best for full, deterministic refreshes — use backups and versioned collection names if you need history. Second, $merge is your atomic update tool: configure into, on, whenMatched, and whenNotMatched to control whether documents are inserted, merged, or replaced. Third, $facet produces a single document whose fields hold arrays from each sub-pipeline; push restrictive filters early to limit memory usage. As a closing reflection, always align your choice of stage with operational needs: durability requirements, the need for incremental updates, memory constraints, and whether downstream consumers expect continuous availability. A short habit to adopt: test pipelines in staging, inspect shapes, and confirm merge semantics before running them against production collections. Key Concepts — Quick Reference means back up before $out, index match keys for $merge, reduce input for $facet; test in staging.. In practical terms, three compact reminders and a closing thought. Module 5 › Chapter 5.6 › Quick Reference
$out
Full overwrite. Use for materialized snapshots. Must be final stage.
$merge
Atomic upserts and merges. Configure on and whenMatched/whenNotMatched.
$facet
Multiple analyses in one query. Watch memory; reduce input first.
Final thought: choose the persistence model that matches your data lifecycle and operational guarantees.
